summary: Defines how to provide NetBIOS services in a TCP/IP environment, for both local networks and internetworks. It describes node types for different topologies, with or without IP broadcast, and explains the ideas and techniques in general terms. Detailed packet specifications are in the companion RFC 1002.

eli5.summary: Some programs speak NetBIOS, an old way of finding and talking to other computers. This memo explains how to make that language work over ordinary Internet connections.

subtitle: How to run the PC-era NetBIOS naming, session and datagram services on top of TCP and UDP.

tldr.problem: NetBIOS was a software interface for personal computers on a shared broadcast medium, with no official protocol standard. Implementations built on the same foundation might not interoperate, and nothing let NetBIOS work across an internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three kinds of end-node (B, P and M) and two kinds of support server (NBNS and NBDD), and maps the NetBIOS name, session and datagram services onto UDP broadcast and unicast, TCP connections, and DNS-style packets.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard with the detailed packet formats in the companion RFC 1002. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 1001 is an Internet Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works as a pair with RFC 1002, which holds the packet formats and constants.

sections.title: What NetBIOS Is and Why It Needed a Standard
sections.content:
RFC 1001 describes the ideas and general methods used to provide NetBIOS on a TCP and UDP foundation. The RFC says NetBIOS had become the dominant mechanism for personal computer networking, giving the IBM Personal Computer and compatibles a vendor independent interface. NetBIOS defines a software interface, not a protocol, and there was no official standard, so the IBM PC Network technical reference served as the reference version.

Protocols that support NetBIOS had been built on many foundations. Even on the same foundation, different implementations might not interoperate without a common protocol. This RFC defines one for TCP and UDP. It also describes a distributed system in which many entities play a part, even ones that are not an end-point of a given connection. The packet formats, protocols and constants are in the companion RFC 1002.

NetBIOS offers three services. The name service lets an application register and release names in a flat name space of sixteen alphanumeric characters. The session service gives reliable, full-duplex, sequenced exchanges of messages from 0 to 131,071 bytes. The datagram service is unreliable and connectionless, and can send to a name or broadcast.
sections.eli5: NetBIOS lets programs on different computers find each other by name, talk reliably, or just toss short notes. This memo says how to do all three using normal Internet tools.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The RFC lists eleven design principles. The most telling ones are: preserve NetBIOS services as the IBM reference defines them (though not every implementation quirk); use existing standards unmodified rather than inventing protocols; minimize options; tolerate errors and disruptions; do not require central management; and allow internet operation.

The disruption principle reflects how NetBIOS networks are used. Computers come on-line at arbitrary times and usually go off-line without telling their peers, so the design cannot depend on a polite shutdown. The RFC also says the standard presupposes that the only broadcast services are those UDP supports, and that multicast is not assumed to be available.

Two principles shape the packet design: require only the minimum necessary to operate, and minimize new inventions. Where an existing protocol almost fits, the RFC prefers to change it a little. That is why the name service follows DNS styles of interaction and packet formats.
sections.eli5: The designers wanted something that keeps working when people just unplug computers, that reuses parts already built, and that needs as few settings as possible.

sections.title: End-Nodes, Servers and Topologies
sections.content:
The standard defines three kinds of end-node, which are the machines that run applications. B (broadcast) nodes use local network broadcasting and directed UDP and TCP, and work within a single broadcast area without any server. P (point-to-point) nodes use only directed UDP datagrams and TCP sessions, never generating or listening for broadcasts, and rely on servers instead. M (mixed mode) nodes are P nodes with some B node behavior: they broadcast first to speed up local lookups, then use servers.

Two kinds of support server are invisible to applications. The NetBIOS Name Server (NBNS) holds name and address information. The NetBIOS Datagram Distribution Server (NBDD) relays datagrams to groups and broadcast, because the internet does not yet support broadcasting or multicasting. An NBNS may act as a mere bulletin board (non-secured) or may monitor names and challenge holders itself (secured), which lets an administrator trade simplicity against security and delay.

A NetBIOS scope is the population of computers across which a registered name is known, identified by a scope identifier that is a valid domain name. The RFC describes three classes of operation: Class 0 is B nodes only, Class 1 is P nodes only, and Class 2 is P and M nodes together. It recommends that a scope contain only B nodes or only P and M nodes, and says B and M nodes should not be mixed in an internet because undetected name conflicts could arise.
sections.eli5: Some computers shout to find each other. Others never shout and ask a directory helper instead. A third kind shouts first and then asks the helper. Mixing the first and third kinds across a big network causes confusion.

sections.title: Representing NetBIOS Names
sections.content:
A NetBIOS name is exactly 16 bytes long as an application sees it. On the wire a longer form is used, built in two levels so that names look like domain names.

In first level encoding, each 4-bit half of every byte is treated as a number and added to the ASCII letter A (hexadecimal 41). The 16-byte name becomes 32 upper-case characters from A to P. A dot and the scope identifier are then appended, which gives a valid domain name. In the RFC's example, the name The NetBIOS name in the scope SCOPE.ID.COM becomes FEGHGFCAEOGFHEECEJEPFDCAHEGBGNGF.SCOPE.ID.COM.

Second level encoding reduces that string to the compressed domain name form defined in RFC 883. Apart from the data in one packet type (the node status response), this second level form is the only name representation used in the packet formats.
sections.eli5: Each letter of the name is chopped in half and each half is written as a letter from A to P. It is a secret-code spelling that looks like an ordinary web-style address.

sections.title: The Name Service
sections.content:
Before a name can be used it must be registered, and afterwards it must be defended against inconsistent registration by others. Before a session or datagram is sent, the holders of the name must be located. A name is either unique (one owner) or group (any number of owners), and that is fixed at registration time, not by the name itself.

Each node type does these jobs differently. B nodes broadcast a claim and win the name if no negative response arrives within the conflict timer. P nodes register through the NBNS. M nodes broadcast first and, if nobody objects, continue as P nodes; only if both claims succeed do they get the name. Lookups work the same way: B nodes broadcast, P nodes ask the NBNS, and M nodes broadcast and then ask the NBNS.

Names held by an NBNS get a lifetime negotiated at registration. The node must send refresh messages before it expires, or the NBNS treats the name as silently released. The NBNS can also challenge a holder by sending a normal name query to it: a positive answer means the node still owns the name, while a negative answer or no answer means it does not. Nodes that detect a name conflict mark the name, after which the only valid user function on it is delete.

Requests are retransmitted if no response arrives in time. The RFC notes that no protocol uses multiple UDP packets for one request or response; if a group list is too big for one UDP packet, a truncation flag tells the node to repeat the query over TCP. A transaction ID, matched together with the partner's IP address, ties responses to requests.
sections.eli5: To get a name you ask around, and if nobody says it is theirs, it is yours. The directory helper may phone the old owner to check they still want it. If they never answer, the name is up for grabs.

sections.title: The Session Service
sections.content:
Session service works the same for all end-node types and uses only directed communication. It has three phases. In establishment, the caller opens a TCP connection to the well-known session port and sends a session request carrying the calling and called NetBIOS names. In the steady state, messages are sent by prepending a message header to the user data and sending both over the TCP connection. In termination, a normal close tries a graceful TCP close first and aborts it if it does not complete in time.

The listener can answer in three ways: accept with a positive response, reject with a negative response and close the connection, or retarget the caller to another IP address and TCP port. Retargeting suits hosts that cannot hand an open TCP connection between processes: a central session server redirects the caller to the application's own port, and the caller places a new call there. For a group name, the caller picks one member from the discovered list and may try another if that fails.

Optional session keep-alive packets help detect a failed peer or network partition. They need no response, and a receiver simply discards them. Since many TCP implementations have their own keep-alive, the RFC recommends the NetBIOS one only when TCP's is absent.
sections.eli5: A session is a phone call. You dial, the other side either picks up, says no, or says call this other number instead. Once connected you talk, and if you sometimes say nothing you can tap the line so you both know it is still there.

sections.title: The Datagram Service
sections.content:
NetBIOS datagrams ride inside UDP packets. Each has a named source and destination, so the sender first performs a name query (or uses a cached answer). A datagram sent to a unique name is unicast, one sent to a group name is multicast, and one sent with the broadcast primitive is broadcast.

A maximum size NetBIOS datagram is 1064 bytes: a 14-byte datagram header plus source and destination names of up to 255 bytes each and at most 512 bytes of user data, inside IP and UDP headers. Since the minimal maximum IP datagram size is 576 bytes, datagrams may be fragmented. Fragments use FIRST and MORE flags and an OFFSET field to be reassembled.

B nodes broadcast datagrams for group names and for the special broadcast name. P and M nodes do not use IP broadcast. They unicast datagrams for unique names directly, but send group and broadcast datagrams to the NBDD, which relays them. A node may first ask the NBDD with a datagram query whether it will relay to a given name. If the NBDD cannot, the node may fetch the owner list from the NBNS and send to each owner itself.
sections.eli5: Datagrams are postcards. A postcard to one person goes straight to them. A postcard to a whole club goes to the club secretary, who passes copies around.
